messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kaito's eyes still widened in his sleep, jolting him awake to scan the darkness for an attacker. It had been two years since he survived the terrorist bombing at the shopping mall where his wife, now ex-wife, was also hurt. The memories of that day - the screams, the smell of smoke and blood, the feeling of helplessness as they were trapped beneath debris - haunted him still. As a bank teller, Kaito's days blurred together in a haze of transactions and customer interactions, but his nights belonged to the past. Kaito had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him; being a loving partner, a supportive friend, or even a calm presence. The trauma had shaken the very foundations of his identity, leaving him feeling lost and uncertain about who he was anymore. This sense of inadequacy made him increasingly irritable, prone to outbursts at work when customers asked too many questions or didn't follow instructions quickly enough. His colleagues began avoiding him, whispering concerns about his 'short fuse' in hushed tones. One evening, as Kaito walked home from the bank, he couldn't shake off the feeling that someone was following him. He frequently looked over his shoulder, his heart racing with every snap of a twig or rustle of leaves. This hypervigilance only intensified when he arrived at his apartment, where he would compulsively check all doors and windows to ensure they were locked. The need for control had become an all-consuming force in Kaito's life. As the weeks went by, Kaito found himself working longer hours to avoid being alone with his thoughts. He would volunteer for extra shifts or take on additional projects just to keep his mind occupied. This excessive work ethic not only strained his relationships with colleagues but also reinforced his growing conviction that he couldn't rely on himself to cope with the trauma. If he wasn't constantly busy, Kaito felt like he was drowning in a sea of anxiety and self-doubt. The more Kaito tried to suppress thoughts about the bombing, the more they seemed to seep into every waking moment. He would catch himself wondering what he could have done differently or replaying the sounds of shattering glass in his mind. These obsessive ruminations chipped away at his already fragile sense of self-worth, fueling further feelings of inadequacy and helplessness. Kaito's divorce had been a slow-motion tragedy, with both partners struggling to reconnect after the trauma. He still remembered the look on his ex-wife's face when she said she couldn't take his anger and withdrawal anymore. It was then that Kaito realized he had also lost intimacy - not just romantic but emotional connection with others in general. The thought of being emotionally close or intimate with someone else now terrified him, and so he pushed people away before they could get too near. It wasn't until a panic attack during work hours left him breathless and ashamed that Kaito realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this - consumed by the past, crippled by fear of the future. As he finally began seeking therapy, Kaito feared most that he might never rediscover himself or learn to trust his own strength again.
